# Abstract {.unnumbered}

# Introduction

Fish populations supply the world’s largest harvest of wild food, supporting livelihoods and nourishing billions of people [@barron2022]. This reliance, together with a history of overexploitation and stock collapses, has motivated decades of monitoring and applied population ecology to inform sustainable fishing practices [@hilborn2020]. Detailed demographic data have proven useful for this task by providing information on the strength of cohorts as they age and the impact of fishing [@hjort1914; @maunder2013]. Fisheries agencies therefore routinely collect age-structured biological and fisheries data for use in stock assessment models.

At their core, age-structured stock assessment models share the demographic logic a Leslie matrix [@leslie1945], a staple model in population ecology, while explicitly accounting for fishing removals [@beverton1957]. They link demographic processes to observations to estimate population trends and project responses to alternative fishing scenarios [@maunder2013]. Since the development of early cohort-reconstruction methods [@fry1949; @gulland1965], fisheries stock assessment has both benefited from and contributed to advances in statistical computing, including early applications of Markov chain Monte Carlo [@lewy2003] and the development of software combining automatic differentiation and Laplace approximation [@fournier2012; @kristensen2016]. These methodological advances are reflected in the development of increasingly sophisticated stock assessment software, including ADAPT [@gavaris1988], Stock Synthesis [@methot2013], SAM [@nielsen2014], WHAM [@stock2021], and FIMS [@stawitz2026].

As stock assessment models and their estimation methods have become more sophisticated, the task of specifying and evaluating alternative model configurations has become increasingly demanding [@punt2020]. For biologists and ecologists familiar with generalized linear and mixed-effects models in R, learning the conventions of specialized assessment software may present a barrier to exploring alternative hypotheses about population, fishing, and observation processes. An interface built around familiar data structures and model formulas could lower this barrier [@jardim2015].

Here we introduce a tiny assessment model, `tinyAM`, an R package designed around such an interface. The package uses tidy tables [@wickham2014] for model inputs and outputs, interactive plots for data exploration and model diagnostics [@regular2020], and formulas to specify assumptions about recruitment, cohort survival, fishing and natural mortality, survey catchability, and observation error. Like the `a4a` framework [@jardim2015], `tinyAM` draws on familiar R modelling conventions, with an emphasis on state-space formulations fit using `RTMB` [@kristensen2026]. Rather than match the full range of capabilities of existing assessment platforms, `tinyAM` prioritizes a compact interface intended to make model assumptions easier to express, modify, and evaluate. We demonstrate the approach by comparing models with fixed and time-varying natural mortality for Northern cod, checking numerical agreement with matched SAM specifications, and translating a collection of assessments from across the North Atlantic and North Pacific.

# The `tinyAM` package

## Population model {#sec-population-model}

### Cohort survival ($N$) {#sec-cohort-survival}

The standard cohort-survival equation lies at the core of `tinyAM`. Population abundance, $N$, is tracked by age, $a$, at the beginning of each year, $y$, and the instantaneous rate of total mortality, $Z_{a,y}$, determines the number of fish surviving to the following year. Survivors advance to the next age or accumulate in the terminal age group, $A$, commonly referred to as the plus group. Specifically,

$$
\widetilde{N}_{a,y+1} =
\begin{cases}
N_{a-1,y}e^{-Z_{a-1,y}}, & a_R<a<A,\\[6pt]
N_{A-1,y}e^{-Z_{A-1,y}}+N_{A,y}e^{-Z_{A,y}}, & a=A
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-cohort}

for $y = y_0,\ldots,Y-1$, where $y_0$ and $Y$ are the first and final years in the model, respectively, $a_R$ is the age at recruitment (the youngest age in the model), and $\widetilde{N}_{a,y+1}$ is the predicted abundance. This equation describes transitions within the age–year matrix, with abundance along two margins specified separately: recruitment in each year ($R_y = N_{a_R,y}$ for $y = y_0,\ldots,Y$; @sec-recruitment) and initial abundance at older ages ($N_{a,y_0}$ for $a = a_R+1,\ldots,A$; @sec-initial-abundance). Total mortality is the sum of fishing mortality (@sec-fishing-mortality) and natural mortality (@sec-natural-mortality): $Z_{a,y}=F_{a,y}+M_{a,y}$.

To account for apparent gains or losses in cohort abundance not explained by fishing or natural mortality, the cohort prediction can be extended to include covariate effects and stochastic deviations,

$$
\log(N_{a,y}) =
\log(\widetilde{N}_{a,y}) +
\mathbf{X}_{N,a,y}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_N +
\eta_{N,a,y},
$$ {#eq-cohort-covariates}

for $a = a_R+1,\ldots,A$ and $y = y_0+1,\ldots,Y$, where $\widetilde{N}_{a,y}$ is the abundance predicted by @eq-cohort. Throughout the model equations, $\mathbf{X}$ denotes a vector of predictor values, $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ a vector of estimated regression coefficients, and $\eta$ a process deviation on the log scale (@sec-process-variation), with subscripts identifying the associated model component and applicable dimensions. Covariate effects and process deviations are optional where supported.

### Initial abundance {#sec-initial-abundance}

Initial abundance at older ages can be specified assuming exponential decay from recruitment in the first year,

$$
N_{a,y_0} = N_{a-1,y_0}e^{-Z_{a-1,y_0}},
\qquad a = a_R+1,\ldots,A.
$$ {#eq-initial-exp}

Alternatively, initial abundances can be estimated as unconstrained parameters, integrated as latent states, or constrained to decline monotonically with age or not exceed initial recruitment.

### Biomass and spawning stock biomass {#sec-biomass}

Beginning-of-year biomass, $B_y$, is calculated as the sum of abundance at age multiplied by supplied stock weights at age, $W_{a,y}$,

$$
B_y = \sum_{a=a_R}^{A} N_{a,y}W_{a,y}.
$$ {#eq-biomass}

Similarly, spawning stock biomass, $S_y$, is calculated as the sum of mature biomass at age, accounting for mortality up to the time of spawning,

$$
S_y = \sum_{a=a_R}^{A} N_{a,y}W_{a,y}P_{a,y}e^{-\tau_{a,y}Z_{a,y}},
$$ {#eq-ssb}

where $P_{a,y}$ is the supplied proportion mature and $\tau_{a,y}$ is the fraction of the year elapsed at spawning. By default, $\tau_{a,y}=0$ and spawning stock biomass corresponds to mature biomass at the beginning of the year.

### Recruitment ($R$) {#sec-recruitment}

Recruitment, $R_y = N_{a_R,y}$, is modelled on the log scale,

$$
\log(R_y) =
\mathbf{X}_{R,y}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_R +
\eta_{R,y},
$$ {#eq-recruitment}

where $\mathbf{X}_{R,y}$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}_R$ define regression effects and $\eta_{R,y}$ is a process deviation (@sec-process-variation).

Recruitment can also be linked to spawning stock biomass by adding $\log[g(S_{y'})]$ to the right-hand side of @eq-recruitment, where $y'=y-\ell$ accounts for the lag between spawning and recruitment (by default, $\ell=a_R$). Supported stock–recruitment functions include Beverton–Holt and Ricker,

$$
g(S_{y'}) =
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{\alpha S_{y'}}{1+\beta S_{y'}},
& \text{Beverton–Holt},\\[8pt]
\alpha S_{y'} e^{-\beta S_{y'}},
& \text{Ricker},
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-stock-recruitment-functions}

with positive parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$. When a stock–recruitment function is specified, the regression intercept is omitted because $\alpha$ governs baseline productivity.

Initial recruitment states (the first year and any subsequent years requiring spawning stock biomass from before the modelled period) are estimated without a recruitment process penalty, either as fixed parameters or as integrated latent states.

### Fishing mortality ($F$) {#sec-fishing-mortality}

For ages subject to fishing, fleet-specific instantaneous fishing mortality rates, $F_{a,y,f}$, are modelled as

$$
\log(F_{a,y,f}) =
\mathbf{X}_{F,a,y,f}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_F +
h_{F,a,y,f} +
\eta_{F,a,y,f},
$$ {#eq-fishing-mortality}

where $\mathbf{X}_{F,a,y,f}$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}_F$ define regression effects and $\eta_{F,a,y,f}$ is a process deviation (@sec-process-variation). Throughout the model equations, $h$ denotes optional structured predictor effects, including Gaussian random effects, parametric selectivity curves, monotonic effects, and penalized smooths (@sec-structured-effects).

For a single fleet or when catches are aggregated across fleets, the fleet subscript is omitted; otherwise, total fishing mortality is $F_{a,y} = \sum_f F_{a,y,f}$. Fishing mortality can also be shared across blocks of ages, requiring predictor components and process deviations to be constant within each block, or fixed at zero for unfished ages.

### Natural mortality ($M$) {#sec-natural-mortality}

Instantaneous rates of natural mortality can be modelled as

$$
\log(M_{a,y}) =
\log(M^{\mathrm{sup}}_{a,y}) +
\mathbf{X}_{M,a,y}^\top\boldsymbol{\beta}_M +
h_{M,a,y} +
\eta_{M,a,y},
$$ {#eq-natural-mortality}

where $M^{\mathrm{sup}}_{a,y}$ is an optionally supplied rate of natural mortality, $\mathbf{X}_{M,a,y}$ and $\boldsymbol{\beta}_M$ define regression effects, $h_{M,a,y}$ represents Gaussian random effects (@sec-structured-effects), and $\eta_{M,a,y}$ is a process deviation (@sec-process-variation). When mortality rates are supplied, the regression intercept is omitted.

As with fishing mortality, ages may be grouped into blocks sharing the same mortality state when process deviations are enabled, requiring supplied rates and predictor components to be constant within each block. Natural mortality deviations can also be restricted to selected ages and years, beginning by default in the second year to reduce potential confounding with initial abundance. Outside these ranges, process deviations are set to zero.

## Statistical components {#sec-statistical-components}

### Process variation {#sec-process-variation}

### Structured effects {#sec-structured-effects}

Structured predictor effects, $h$, provide additional flexibility beyond ordinary regression effects. These include Gaussian random effects, parametric curves, monotonic effects, and penalized smooths, described below using general notation applicable to the relevant model components.

#### Gaussian random effects

Gaussian random effects can be included in predictors for fishing mortality, natural mortality, survey catchability, and observation-error scales,

$$
h_i^{\mathrm{Gaussian}} = z_i u_{g_i,k_i},
$$ {#eq-gaussian-effects}

where $i$ indexes a predictor row, $k_i$ identifies the effect level, and $g_i$ identifies an optional grouping factor. The multiplier $z_i$ is one unless a covariate is supplied to model random slopes. Within each group, effects follow a one-dimensional IID, RW or AR1 process (@sec-process-variation), with the first RW effect fixed at zero. Group-specific trajectories are independent but share process parameters. Specifying the variance of a Gaussian effect allows prior information to be incorporated. For example, adding a Gaussian effect with a specified variance to the logarithm of a supplied natural mortality rate induces a lognormal prior on natural mortality.

#### Parametric curves

Fishing mortality and survey catchability can be structured using parametric selectivity curves. For a numeric predictor, $x$ (e.g., age), supported curves include

$$
\begin{aligned}
h^{\mathrm{curve}}(x) &= \log[s(x)],\\[8pt]
s(x) &=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{1+e^{-k(x-x_{50})}},
& \text{Logistic},\\[12pt]
\displaystyle
\frac{1}{1+e^{-(x-x_{50}^{\uparrow})/w^{\uparrow}}}
\frac{1}{1+e^{(x-x_{50}^{\downarrow})/w^{\downarrow}}},
& \text{Double logistic},\\[12pt]
\displaystyle
e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-x_{\mathrm{peak}}}{w}\right)^2},
& \text{Normal}.
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-selectivity-curves}

The curve parameters define locations ($x_{50}$ and $x_{\mathrm{peak}}$), slopes ($k$), and widths ($w$), with slopes and widths constrained to be positive. Curve parameters may differ among groups, such as fleets or surveys. Curves act as multiplicative effects on fishing mortality or catchability, contributing to their log-scale predictors. The double-logistic curve is not rescaled to have a maximum of one.

#### Monotonic effects

A monotonic relationship for fishing mortality or catchability can be specified using cumulative non-negative increments,

$$
h_i^{\mathrm{mono}} =
\sum_{j=1}^{k_i-1}d_j,
\qquad d_j\geq 0,
$$ {#eq-monotonic-selectivity}

where $i$ indexes a predictor row, $k_i$ is the position of its predictor value among ordered levels, and $d_j$ is an estimated increment on the predictor scale. This formulation allows relationships to increase or plateau without imposing a parametric curve.

#### Penalized smooths

As in the `a4a` framework [@jardim2015], penalized smooths can be used to describe fishing mortality. Smooths can also be included in predictors for survey catchability and observation-error scales. Following the implementation in `sdmTMB` [@anderson2025], `tinyAM` uses `mgcv` [@wood2017] to construct spline bases and represent penalized coefficients as Gaussian random effects. The penalized contribution takes the general form

$$
h_i^{\mathrm{smooth}} =
\sum_j \mathbf{b}_{j,i}^\top\mathbf{u}_j,
\qquad
\mathbf{u}_j \sim
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma_{u,j}^2\mathbf{I}),
$$ {#eq-penalized-smooths}

where $\mathbf{b}_{j,i}$ is a vector of basis function values and $\mathbf{u}_j$ is a vector of penalized coefficients. Unpenalized basis components are included in the linear predictor. Both univariate and tensor-product smooths are supported, with smoothness estimated during model fitting.
